title: AWS EC2 Pricing Explained: A 2026 Guide to Costs
summary: AWS EC2 pricing depends on payment model choice more than instance size. You'll see how On-Demand, Reserved, and Spot options affect your monthly bill.
body_markdown:
## Automate EC2 cost alerts and shutdowns with Activepieces


Activepieces won't make EC2 cheaper.


It can keep a small team from paying for instances nobody is using, by sending cost alerts to a person and stopping dev machines on a schedule, and the free plan on Activepieces Cloud, $0 with 1,000 credits a month, is enough to run both, so the cost isn't a barrier to implementation.


Nobody notices until the invoice arrives that an idle instance still bills for its storage and its public IPv4 address. A workflow that taps someone on the shoulder, or switches the machine off, costs far less than that surprise.


### Budget alert to Slack with owner and cost


When spending crosses a line you set, AWS Budgets can already warn you. On its own, that warning lands in an inbox where it gets ignored.


Activepieces takes that alert and posts it where people actually read, and Slack is one of its 747 integrations, along with the name of the person responsible and the amount spent, which means the alert hits a platform your team already uses.


Describe that alert-to-Slack flow in the built-in chat and what comes back is a published flow in your account, the same artifact a builder would assemble by hand, running under the same RBAC and audit logs as every other flow.


Its run trace lists each step in order, so the Budgets alert, the Slack post and the owner's name in the message can all be read back after the fact. Flows are unlimited on every plan, including free, so a trial costs nothing.


In the flow below the shape is the same: an event arrives, and a message goes to a Slack channel. Here the trigger is a failed Stripe payment, but you swap in the budget alert and the structure stays identical.


To confirm a message went out rather than assume it did, look at the run details on the left, which show the step finished.


Spend your time on the message. Put the account or project, the amount, and the owner's name in it, so the reader knows whose money it is and doesn't have to ask.


An alert that says "budget exceeded" gets a shrug. One that names a person gets an answer.


### Scheduled stop and start of tagged instances


On a timer, the second flow looks for instances carrying a tag such as` environment=dev` , asks a person to approve, and only then stops them.


Stopping at night and starting in the morning means a development box isn't billing compute while everyone sleeps. Storage keeps billing either way, so this trims one line of the bill, not all of it.


Skip the approval and a stopped instance someone was relying on becomes a worse problem than the saving. Tags matter for the same reason: the flow touches only what you marked, and leaves production alone.


Give the AWS credentials Activepieces uses only the permissions the job needs, and on a self-hosted instance you can keep those keys in your own secret manager instead of the Activepieces database:


- Permission to describe instances, so the flow can find the tagged ones
- Permission to stop instances
- Permission to start instances
- Read access to Budgets, if the flow pulls cost figures itself


Scope the stop and start permissions to the dev tag in the policy, so a mistake in the workflow can't reach a machine you never meant to touch.
